paragraphs: Choosing which language model handles a query can change both answer quality and computational cost. Routing makes that choice once, selecting a single model. Cascading instead tries models sequentially, moving to larger ones until an answer is considered satisfactory. This paper studies how to make these decisions within a common framework.

The authors derive an optimal cascading strategy and prove the optimality of an existing routing strategy. They then introduce cascade routing, which combines both forms of selection into a strategy with a theoretical optimality result. The contribution therefore includes both decision rules and an analysis of why those rules work within the studied formulation.

A central finding is that model selection depends critically on good quality estimators: the system needs useful estimates of how well models will answer. In the reported experiments, cascade routing consistently surpasses either approach alone by a large margin. The analysis of quality estimators also helps identify when routing, cascading, or their combination can improve the cost-performance tradeoff.
icml-2025-a-unified-approach-to-routing-.tldr: Cascade routing combines model routing and sequential escalation, with theoretical optimality results and strong experimental gains tied to quality estimation.

paragraphs: Data attribution asks how individual training examples affect a model’s predictions. Influence functions offer a way to estimate that effect without repeatedly retraining the model. However, their common machine-learning derivation assumes that the training objective separates into individual example losses. Objectives involving relationships among examples, such as contrastive and ranking losses, do not fit that form.

The authors return to a more general formulation from robust statistics and develop the Versatile Influence Function, or VIF. Its intended scope includes models trained with any non-decomposable loss. By building the method around automatic differentiation, they avoid requiring a separate mathematical derivation for each particular loss function.

The paper evaluates VIF on survival analysis with Cox regression, network analysis with node embeddings, and information retrieval with listwise ranking. Across these examples, its influence estimates closely resemble those obtained by removing an example and retraining. Computation is up to 1,000 times faster, supporting its usefulness as an efficient approximation to that expensive attribution procedure.
icml-2025-a-versatile-influence-function.tldr: VIF extends efficient training-data attribution to coupled loss functions, closely matching leave-one-out retraining in three evaluated applications.

paragraphs: Running a neural network repeatedly involves multiplying inputs by its weight matrices. This paper focuses on networks whose weights take binary or ternary values. Its starting observation is that trained weights remain fixed during inference, making it possible to prepare a more efficient representation before processing inputs.

The proposed algorithms preprocess these matrices and construct indices that support faster multiplication while reducing storage requirements by a logarithmic factor. For an n-by-n weight matrix, the stated multiplication time is O(n²/log n), a logarithmic improvement over standard vector-matrix multiplication. The method therefore exploits both the restricted weight values and the opportunity to reuse preprocessing.

Experiments assess whether these theoretical savings translate into practical benefits. The authors report multiplication speedups of up to 29 times and memory reductions of up to six times. Applied to language models, the algorithms achieve inference speedups of up to 5.24 times. These are reported maxima across the experiments, and the full-model result measures a different scope from the multiplication result.
icml-2025-an-efficient-matrix-multiplica.tldr: Preprocessing fixed binary and ternary weights enables faster, smaller matrix operations and reported language-model inference speedups of up to 5.24 times.

paragraphs: Synthetic medical data can supplement scarce observations, but its usefulness depends on which examples are generated and how they are used. Profile2Gen addresses this problem by concentrating on hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks, where a model predicts a numerical outcome. The focus is on improving the training data through guided generation and refinement.

The framework takes a data-centric approach: difficulties in the samples guide efforts to improve the synthetic dataset. The authors also extend DataIQ to regression, broadening a framework for examining data beyond its previous scope. Together, these contributions connect the assessment of learning difficulty with the construction of more useful training examples.

The evaluation includes approximately 18,000 experiments across six medical datasets and seven generative models. The results indicate that refined synthetic samples can lower prediction errors and improve model reliability. Statistical analyses find performance equal to or better than training exclusively on real data. These findings support targeted refinement as a useful part of synthetic-data generation in the evaluated medical regression tasks.
icml-2025-breaking-the-barrier-of-hard-s.tldr: Profile2Gen guides synthetic medical data generation toward hard-to-learn regression samples, achieving equal or better performance than real-data-only training in its evaluation.

paragraphs: Bayesian decision making uses observations to form beliefs about an unknown data-generating process. Minimizing average risk under those beliefs can still produce poor decisions when the model is uncertain or observations are limited and noisy. This paper introduces DRO-BAS, which instead minimizes worst-case risk across a set of distributions informed by the posterior.

The authors construct two versions of this ambiguity set: one based on posterior expectations and another based on the posterior predictive distribution. Under stated conditions, both have strong dual formulations that yield efficient, single-stage stochastic optimization problems. These are solved by approximating expectations with sample averages.

The theoretical coverage differs between the two versions. The posterior-expectation formulation covers all conjugate exponential-family members, while the posterior-predictive result requires conditions on its moment generating function. In experiments, the methods outperform existing Bayesian distributionally robust optimization on the Newsvendor problem. On portfolio optimization, they solve faster while providing comparable robustness, connecting the mathematical reformulation to practical decision-making efficiency.
icml-2025-decision-making-under-the-expo.tldr: DRO-BAS uses Bayesian beliefs to define worst-case decision problems with conditional tractability guarantees and favorable results on inventory and portfolio tasks.

paragraphs: Discrepancy minimization assigns a plus or minus sign to each column of a matrix so that every row’s signed sum stays small. The objective is to reduce the largest absolute row sum. This paper accelerates approximate solutions for real-valued matrices while preserving the approximation guarantee of an earlier combinatorial algorithm.

For a matrix with m rows and n columns, the first algorithm runs in roughly nnz(A) + n³ time, with logarithmic factors suppressed; nnz(A) counts nonzero entries. A further version uses fast matrix multiplication to reduce the n-dependent term to n²·⁵³. This breaks the cubic runtime barrier for square matrices.

Two technical ideas drive the improvement: a sketching method using implicit leverage-score sampling, and a data structure that accelerates iterative partial coloring. The latter supports delayed batch updates with low-rank corrections. The results move the cost closer to processing the nonzero input itself and nearly close the computational gap between discrepancy algorithms for real-valued and binary matrices.
icml-2025-discrepancy-minimization-in-in.tldr: New sketching and update techniques accelerate approximate discrepancy minimization while preserving an existing approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by reversing a process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data. Accurately following that reverse process usually requires many small steps, making generation expensive. This paper changes what the model learns so that it can take larger steps while retaining useful information about possible clean outputs.

Instead of predicting only the average clean sample associated with a noisy input, the method learns the full conditional distribution of clean samples. The authors replace the usual regression objective with a scoring rule, allowing training to target a distribution rather than just its mean. That distribution supports sampling the reverse process’s transitions over a coarser time scale.

The approach is evaluated on image generation and robot trajectory generation. With few discretization steps, it consistently outperforms standard diffusion models in the reported experiments. The authors describe substantial acceleration with minimal output-quality degradation. The central finding is that learning uncertainty over clean samples can make larger reverse-process steps more useful, reducing the need for many fine-grained denoising updates.
icml-2025-distributional-diffusion-model.tldr: Learning distributions of clean samples instead of conditional means enables faster diffusion generation with strong results at few sampling steps.

paragraphs: Macro placement determines where large modules sit within an integrated circuit, influencing chip performance. Existing search methods can spend substantial computation rebuilding layouts, making random changes, or evaluating placement masks. EGPlace addresses these costs within an evolutionary optimization framework that combines guided changes with efficient layout reconstruction.

Its first innovation is a mutation operator guided by greedy repositioning. This operator identifies critical regions of a layout and directs changes toward improving them, making exploration more targeted. Its second innovation is an efficient mask computation algorithm that accelerates layout evaluation. Together, these mechanisms address both the usefulness of proposed changes and the cost of assessing them.

On the ISPD2005 and Ariane RISC-V CPU benchmarks, EGPlace reduces wirelength by 10.8% relative to WireMask-EA and 9.3% relative to EfficientPlace, a reinforcement-learning placement method. It also achieves respective speedups of 7.8 and 2.8 times. These results indicate that the evaluated framework improves placement quality while reducing computation, rather than requiring more search time to obtain shorter wiring.
icml-2025-egplace-an-efficient-macro-pla.tldr: EGPlace combines targeted evolutionary changes with faster layout evaluation to reduce both wirelength and placement runtime in chip-design benchmarks.

paragraphs: Outsourcing language-model computation to a cloud provider reduces the client’s computational burden but can expose the query. Fully homomorphic encryption provides a way to compute on an encrypted query while keeping the result encrypted as well. The client holding the secret key can recover the result without giving the cloud provider access to the query’s contents.

EncryptedLLM develops a GPU-accelerated implementation of this encryption technology and uses it to execute an encrypted GPT-2 forward pass. The reported runtime is more than 200 times faster than the CPU baseline. This comparison concerns encrypted computation on the two hardware implementations; its significance is a substantial reduction in the cost of performing the protected forward pass.

The work also experimentally studies approximations to language-model activation functions. These approximations are part of maintaining accuracy while achieving the reported performance. The contribution therefore combines accelerated encrypted execution with analysis of how to adapt model operations, addressing both computational speed and the accuracy of the resulting encrypted inference.
icml-2025-encryptedllm-privacy-preservin.tldr: EncryptedLLM accelerates an encrypted GPT-2 forward pass by over 200 times against a CPU baseline while studying accuracy-preserving activation approximations.

paragraphs: Running reinforcement-learning agents in parallel speeds up data collection, but identical agents may repeatedly gather similar experiences. This paper asks whether specializing their policies can make parallel collection more useful than simply increasing the number of copies. The focus is on diversity in the collected data, alongside the volume of experience.

The proposed framework maximizes data entropy by balancing two considerations: how broadly each individual agent explores and how different the agents are from one another. A centralized policy-gradient method implements the diversity component. This balance aims to reduce redundant experiences while retaining exploration within each agent’s own behavior.

Empirical comparisons with identical-agent systems show promise, including compatibility with batch reinforcement-learning techniques that can benefit from diverse data. The authors also provide a concentration analysis showing faster rates for specialized parallel sampling distributions. That theoretical result supports the sampling strategy, while the experimental claims remain qualified: the abstract does not establish a universal speedup beyond the number of parallel agents.
icml-2025-enhancing-diversity-in-paralle.tldr: Specializing parallel agents to balance individual exploration and collective diversity shows promise for reducing redundant reinforcement-learning data.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks simulate physical systems by exchanging information among nodes of a mesh. Hierarchical graphs help them represent relationships at multiple scales, but these hierarchies are often manually designed and fixed. EvoMesh makes the hierarchy itself learnable so that information exchange can adapt to the physical system’s evolving dynamics.

The framework jointly learns physical dynamics and graph hierarchies through a fully differentiable process. Within each hierarchy, anisotropic message passing aggregates features differently according to direction. At the same time, the model learns probabilities for selecting nodes at the next hierarchical level, using the physical context to guide those choices.

This design creates more flexible shortcuts for messages and strengthens the model’s ability to capture long-range dependencies. Experiments on five physical-simulation benchmark datasets show large improvements over recent message-passing networks with fixed hierarchies. The stated results support adapting the structure used for computation alongside the simulated dynamics, rather than treating the hierarchy as a permanently chosen part of the model.
icml-2025-evomesh-adaptive-physical-simu.tldr: EvoMesh jointly learns physical dynamics and adaptive graph hierarchies, outperforming fixed-hierarchy networks on five simulation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Rectified-flow models can generate images quickly, but editing an existing image also requires an effective reverse operation. Inversion maps the image back to structured noise, providing a starting point for reconstruction and subsequent changes. FireFlow addresses fast, accurate inversion and semantic editing without additional training.

The method centers on a carefully designed numerical solver for rectified-flow inversion. The authors report accuracy associated with a second-order solver while retaining the practical efficiency of a first-order Euler method. This matters because errors in the inversion affect how accurately the original image can be reconstructed before an edit is applied.

FireFlow extends models such as FLUX to inversion and editing in eight steps. Compared with state-of-the-art rectified-flow inversion and editing techniques, the solver delivers a threefold runtime speedup, smaller reconstruction errors, and better editing results in the reported evaluation. The contribution shows how changing the numerical procedure can improve both speed and reconstruction quality while using the existing model’s capabilities in a zero-shot, training-free setting.
icml-2025-fireflow-fast-inversion-of-rec.tldr: FireFlow enables training-free rectified-flow inversion and image editing in eight steps, with reported improvements in speed, reconstruction, and editing quality.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning adapts a language model using training examples from a target domain. When only a fixed number of examples can be used, choosing the subset becomes part of the efficiency problem. FisherSFT addresses this choice by seeking examples that maximize information gain under a mathematical criterion tied to the fine-tuning objective.

The criterion uses the Fisher information matrix, which supplies the paper’s measure of informativeness. To make selection efficient, the authors approximate this quantity through a linearization at the model’s last layer. This approximation connects a theoretically analyzable selection rule to a computation intended to be practical for language-model fine-tuning.

The authors report favorable empirical performance on several problems, using both quantitative measurements and language-model judgments. The contribution is therefore a method for allocating a fixed training-example budget more effectively, supported by analysis and experiments. Its stated findings suggest that selecting examples by their information contribution can improve the efficiency of adaptation without requiring the selection procedure to handle the full model in the same way.
icml-2025-fishersft-data-efficient-super.tldr: FisherSFT selects informative fine-tuning examples using an efficient last-layer approximation to a Fisher-information-based selection criterion.

paragraphs: This paper improves model-based reinforcement learning for Craftax-classic, an open-world survival game requiring exploration, generalization, and long-term reasoning. The approach targets sample efficiency: learning strong behavior from a limited number of interactions with the environment. It begins with a strong model-free policy architecture that combines convolutional and recurrent neural networks.

The authors then introduce three changes to the model-based setup. Dyna with warmup trains the policy using both real experience and imagined data. A nearest-neighbor tokenizer changes how image patches become inputs to the transformer world model. Block teacher forcing allows that world model to reason jointly about the future tokens belonging to the next timestep.

After one million environment steps, the method reaches a reported reward of 69.66%, compared with 53.2% for DreamerV3 and 65.0% for human performance. The authors describe this as a new state of the art and the first result above human performance on the benchmark. The findings connect improvements in policy design, imagined training, and world-model representation to more efficient learning in this setting.
icml-2025-improving-transformer-world-mo.tldr: Policy and transformer world-model improvements achieve 69.66% reward on Craftax-classic after one million environment steps, exceeding the reported human benchmark.

paragraphs: Representation fine-tuning steers a language model by learning interventions in its internal representations during a forward pass. Existing pointwise approaches apply transformations within a concept subspace. This paper extends that idea to distributions, so the learned intervention accounts for surrounding regions of the subspace as well as individual points.

The change broadens what the intervention learns about the representation space. Instead of limiting control to pointwise transformations, it incorporates variation around them. The authors find that these distribution-wise methods work effectively in early model layers. They also observe a strong correlation between larger standard deviations and improved performance; this is reported as an association, rather than a universal causal rule.

Evaluation covers eight commonsense-reasoning and seven arithmetic-reasoning benchmarks. Across these tests, distribution-wise interventions consistently outperform pointwise interventions in controllability and robustness. The findings support using distributions as a richer basis for steering model behavior, with evidence that useful control can occur early in the model and remain effective across the evaluated reasoning tasks.
icml-2025-learning-distribution-wise-con.tldr: Distribution-wise representation interventions improve language-model controllability and robustness over pointwise interventions across fifteen reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization seeks solutions with few nonzero entries, but applications often impose additional constraints. Enforcing both kinds together can require a difficult projection onto their intersection. This paper studies additional constraints that preserve support and replaces that joint projection with a customized sequence of two projections.

The authors incorporate the two-step operator into a variant of iterative hard thresholding. Their analysis introduces a tradeoff between relaxing sparsity and accepting suboptimality in the objective value. Under restricted strong-convexity and smoothness assumptions, the algorithm has global objective-value guarantees in deterministic, stochastic, and zeroth-order settings. These are conditional guarantees involving the stated tradeoff, rather than an unconditional claim of exact optimization.

A central proof contribution extends the classic three-point lemma to the two-step nonconvex projection operator, enabling the convergence analysis. In the zeroth-order setting, the technique also removes a persistent error term from a previous result, even without extra constraints. The work thus contributes both a simpler constraint-handling procedure and analysis that strengthens what can be guaranteed about its output.
icml-2025-optimization-over-sparse-suppo.tldr: A two-step projection method handles sparse support-preserving constraints with conditional global objective guarantees and an explicit sparsity–suboptimality tradeoff.

paragraphs: Predicting how a mutation changes protein binding is useful for structural biology and therapeutic design. The paper notes that deep-learning predictors have lagged behind expensive empirical force-field estimates, possibly because binding measurements are scarce. Its response is to transfer information from protein sequence modeling and folding-stability prediction.

The key formulation expresses binding energy as the folding energy of the protein complex minus the combined folding energies of its separate partners. This connects the target prediction to folding-energy estimates. A pretrained inverse-folding model serves as a proxy for those energies, producing strong zero-shot performance before task-specific fine-tuning.

The model can then be fine-tuned using abundant folding-energy measurements alongside the smaller supply of binding-energy measurements. The resulting predictor, StaB-ddG, matches the accuracy of FoldX while offering a speedup greater than 1,000 times in the reported comparison. The authors describe it as the first deep-learning predictor to reach that accuracy level, showing how related measurements can help address limited binding data.
icml-2025-predicting-mutational-effects-.tldr: StaB-ddG transfers folding-energy knowledge to mutation-induced binding predictions, matching FoldX accuracy with a reported speedup exceeding 1,000 times.

paragraphs: In procurement auctions, a buyer acquires services from sellers who know their own costs. This paper assumes that service quality is measured by a known submodular function. The objective is to approximately maximize quality minus sellers’ total costs while supporting truthful participation, individual rationality for sellers, and nonnegative surplus for the buyer.

The authors improve analysis of algorithms for non-positive submodular maximization and develop frameworks that convert optimization algorithms into auction mechanisms. These conversions preserve approximation guarantees alongside the required economic properties. They cover both offline auctions and online settings where sellers arrive in an adversarial order and purchase decisions cannot be reversed.

The paper also studies descending-price auctions with adversarial price schedules. It shows that an optimization algorithm meeting a particular two-part welfare guarantee can be converted into such an auction, and connects descending auctions to online submodular optimization. Experiments instantiate the frameworks with existing algorithms on public datasets containing thousands of sellers. This links algorithmic approximation results to mechanisms that account for strategic behavior.
icml-2025-procurement-auctions-via-appro.tldr: The paper converts submodular optimization algorithms into efficient procurement auctions while preserving approximation guarantees and key incentive properties.

paragraphs: Generative models typically reproduce patterns in existing data, while exploration seeks novel possibilities. This paper formulates exploration as maximizing entropy over the approximate data manifold represented by a pretrained diffusion model. That formulation uses the model’s learned structure to define where exploration takes place without relying on explicit uncertainty quantification.

The authors first develop an exploration principle based on density estimation, then address the practical difficulty of estimating those densities. They use a connection between the entropy of a diffusion model’s induced distribution and its score function. This leads to a mirror-descent algorithm that implements exploration through sequential fine-tuning of the pretrained model.

The paper proves convergence to the optimal exploratory diffusion model under its stated assumptions, drawing on analysis of mirror flows. Experiments on synthetic data and high-dimensional text-to-image diffusion show promising results. The contribution combines a mathematically defined exploration objective with an algorithm using diffusion-model quantities, while the convergence claim remains conditional and the empirical findings are presented as promising rather than universal.
icml-2025-provable-maximum-entropy-manif.tldr: Sequential diffusion-model fine-tuning maximizes exploratory entropy on a learned manifold, with conditional convergence guarantees and promising empirical results.

paragraphs: When reliable observations are scarce or expensive, model predictions can provide additional information for statistical estimation. Existing hybrid methods combine a small observed dataset with many imputed outputs, but often target only an average or a single quantile. QuEst extends this approach to a wider family of measures describing a distribution.

The framework produces both point estimates and rigorous confidence intervals for quantile-based quantities. Its scope includes tail-risk measures such as CVaR and population segments such as quartiles. This matters when the quantity of interest concerns a particular part of a distribution rather than its overall average, while uncertainty about the estimate still needs to be quantified.

The authors also extend QuEst to multidimensional metrics and introduce an optimization technique to further reduce variance in QuEst and other hybrid estimators. Experiments cover economic modeling, opinion polling, and language-model auto-evaluation. These applications demonstrate the usefulness of combining observed and predicted data for a broader range of statistical questions, with uncertainty intervals included as part of the estimation framework.
icml-2025-quest-enhancing-estimates-of-q.tldr: QuEst combines observed data and model predictions to estimate diverse quantile-based measures with rigorous confidence intervals.

paragraphs: A visual reinforcement-learning agent must extract useful state information from images before it can make good decisions. Measuring that ability is difficult when benchmarks change visual demands together with other learning challenges. Sliding Puzzles Gym adapts the classic tile puzzle into a benchmark designed to isolate and scale the representation-learning problem.

The benchmark draws puzzle images from potentially very large datasets and offers controls through grid sizes and image pools. Its stated design separates changes in representation complexity from the environment’s dynamics, observation space, and action space. Researchers can therefore examine how increasing visual diversity affects learning within a controlled decision-making task.

Experiments include both model-free and model-based algorithms. As the image pool grows, every tested algorithm loses performance both within and outside the training distribution. More sophisticated representation techniques often do worse than simpler methods such as data augmentation. These findings expose weaknesses in the evaluated methods’ handling of visual diversity and make the benchmark useful for studying representation learning separately from broader reinforcement-learning performance.
icml-2025-sliding-puzzles-gym-a-scalable.tldr: Sliding Puzzles Gym isolates visual representation challenges and reveals declining performance across tested reinforcement-learning algorithms as image diversity increases.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery uses knowledge of known classes to identify both familiar and new categories in unlabeled data. This paper introduces that task for graphs and studies when old categories can help discover new ones. Its theoretical focus is parametric category discovery, extending analysis beyond the non-graph settings addressed by existing methods.

The authors measure the relationship between old and new classes in the embedding space using Wasserstein distance. They derive a loss bound based on that distance and identify two necessary conditions for effective discovery. Through a pairwise Markov random field perspective, they then show that popular graph contrastive-learning methods inherently violate those conditions.

To address this mismatch, the paper proposes SWIRL, a graph contrastive-learning method designed for category discovery. Experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution connects the geometry of learned representations to the usefulness of known classes, then uses that analysis to motivate a new method; the identified necessary conditions are not presented as sufficient guarantees of success.
icml-2025-towards-understanding-parametr.tldr: A Wasserstein-based analysis identifies necessary conditions for graph category discovery and motivates the experimentally supported SWIRL method.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo tree search is an effective reinforcement-learning planner, but scaling it across parallel computation is challenging. Sequential Monte Carlo offers an alternative based on particles. This paper argues that design choices inherited from particle-filter smoothing can conflict with online planning’s immediate objective: improving the policy at the point where planning begins.

Trust-Region Twisted SMC adapts the planner to that objective. Inspired by tree search, it changes how planning data are generated through constrained action sampling and explicit treatment of terminal states. It also improves the estimation of policy and value targets, addressing both the experiences produced inside planning and the information extracted from them.

The resulting TRT-SMC method improves runtime and sample efficiency relative to the evaluated tree-search and SMC baselines in both discrete and continuous domains. The findings support tailoring particle-based planning to reinforcement learning’s policy-improvement goal. The contribution is therefore a coordinated redesign of the planner, rather than only a change to how many particles or simulations it uses.
icml-2025-trust-region-twisted-policy-im.tldr: TRT-SMC tailors particle-based planning to immediate policy improvement, achieving better runtime and sample efficiency than evaluated MCTS and SMC baselines.

paragraphs: Continual-learning systems can forget earlier tasks when learning new ones. Rehearsal addresses this by retaining some past data, usually mixing it with current-task data during training. This paper asks whether the order of rehearsal matters and whether revisiting old tasks sequentially can sometimes work better than training everything together.

The authors analyze overparameterized linear models and explicitly characterize forgetting and generalization error. They compare concurrent rehearsal with a sequential strategy that learns new data first and then revisits past tasks. Their analysis shows an advantage for sequential rehearsal when tasks are less similar, making task relationships central to the choice of training schedule.

That result motivates Hybrid Rehearsal, which trains similar tasks together and revisits dissimilar tasks sequentially. The paper characterizes its forgetting and generalization behavior and evaluates the idea with deep neural networks. Those experiments find that the hybrid method outperforms standard concurrent rehearsal. The theoretical results apply to the analyzed linear models, while the neural-network experiments provide additional empirical support for adapting rehearsal order to task similarity.
icml-2025-unlocking-the-power-of-rehears.tldr: Analysis links rehearsal effectiveness to task similarity and motivates a hybrid schedule that outperforms concurrent rehearsal in neural-network experiments.

paragraphs: Some data occupy curved geometric spaces, so statistical modeling benefits from accounting for that structure. This paper focuses on the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices. It develops a version of the Gaussian distribution suited to that space, bringing a familiar statistical model into a setting where the underlying geometry matters.

The authors construct a non-isotropic wrapped Gaussian using the exponential map. Non-isotropy allows the distribution’s spread to vary by direction. They derive theoretical properties and provide a maximum-likelihood framework for estimating parameters, giving the proposed distribution both a mathematical foundation and a procedure for fitting it to data.

The paper also interprets existing classifiers for these matrices probabilistically and introduces classifiers based on the new wrapped Gaussian. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate robustness and flexibility. These findings support the distribution as a tool for geometry-aware analysis, while the broader contribution is a basis for extending classical statistical modeling and classification to this structured matrix space.
icml-2025-wrapped-gaussian-on-the-manifo.tldr: A non-isotropic wrapped Gaussian provides geometry-aware estimation and classification for symmetric positive definite matrices.
